It is analogous to Jev , the System One model from TypeSafe AI. While browsing Hacker News, I stumbled upon What music does Gemini Decision 1 like? by Liam Warfield. He ends the article with a few ideas to extend his project. The last of these suggestions, “Does it [Gemini Decision 1] like or hate AI-generated music?”, stood out to me because it implicitly suggests that the decision model may be able to recognize AI-generated audio. As it turns out, Gemini Decision 1 can separate AI voices from human voices well above chance, but only if the AI voice generator was published before 2025. As a quick clarification, I am saying separates rather than categorizes as the model has a strong bias towards labeling all tested audio as human-made. Out of 1,020 AI clips, only 20 were given a 50% or higher chance of being AI-generated. However, the ROC-AUC chance that a random AI clip is assigned a higher P(AI) than a random human clip was significantly higher in pre-2025 models, suggesting that recent AI voices are less distinguishable than before. Each point is an AI voice generator, measured by how well Gemini Decision 1 separates 30 of its audio clips from 200 human audiobook clips. When pooled together, generators from 2023 and 2024 are separated with an AUC of 0.67. Six older generators, from 2017 to 2022, score the same (0.67). However, generators released in 2025 and 2026 have an AUC of only 0.52, effectively chance. All but one of the 2025-2026 generators have a 95% confidence interval that includes 0.5; the only exception, Inworld TTS-2, has a confidence interval of 0.51-0.75. Each clip was scored with a Simple Noul binary question with output between 0 and 1 , Criteria Noul Simple Noul with provided criteria for context , and 5-Pt Rubric rescaled score from “Definitely authentic human recording” to “Definitely AI-generated or synthetic” . Notably, rather than gently sloping downward, we observe that AUC drops sharply at the end of 2024, or the start of 2025. The generators that fooled people also tended to fool Gemini Decision 1 (r = +0.57), but they do not always align. Generative reasoning is reshaping how ranking and decision systems work. Models like GR2 (Generative Reasoning Re-ranker) [ arXiv:2606.31984 ] have demonstrated that generative reasoning can meaningfully improve re-ranking quality. The next question is: for large-scale ranking and decision systems, how small can the policy model be without losing that generative reasoning capability? A 0.6B dense student distilled from stronger teachers could serve with much lower latency and cost, enabling broader traffic coverage, faster model refreshes, and more RL experiments per day. That requires the whole training cycle to be fast, and model FLOPs are only one part of it. At 0.6B parameters, rollout generation, synchronization, and framework overhead take a growing share of wall-clock time. Because a 0.6B model has far less matrix arithmetic per layer than frontier dense or MoE models, fixed system overheads (host dispatch, synchronization, and KV-cache lifecycle) shift the bottleneck from FLOPs to coordination. We ran RL for a 0.6-billion-parameter model on a 64-chip Google Cloud TPU v7 (Ironwood) slice. The model has far fewer weights than the large dense and mixture-of-experts systems that usually motivate distributed training work, and its small size made the workload hard to run efficiently. For a large dense or MoE model, each layer performs enough matrix computation that device utilization is often dominated by the familiar questions: how to shard parameters, move activations, route experts, and keep large matrix units busy. Those problems are hard, but their costs scale visibly with the model. A small dense model changes the balance. The useful matrix work per device shrinks, but many fixed costs do not: As the model gets smaller, these fixed costs take a larger share of each step. A few milliseconds of dispatch overhead, an overly large attention compute block, or a cache allocation repeated on every update could dominate the work we wanted TPU v7 to perform. Small dense-model RL is therefore a coordination-sensitive workload with its own bottlenecks, and it benefits from hardware-software-model co-design. story|title:how packaged clean rooms bri.content_excerpt: A look at how LiveRamp Embedded Identity runs inside Databricks Clean Rooms: the central clean room, how OpenSharing connects each party's data, who can see what, and where the results land. Historically on Databricks, to resolve customer records to a person-based ID such as RampID, a data team had to export PII to an outside service, wait for a match file, and load it back in. Each step added a pipeline to maintain, a copy of sensitive data to govern, and a delay before the results were usable. Packaged clean rooms disrupt this traditional pattern by removing the need for that round-trip. LiveRamp Embedded Identity on Databricks brings the identity service to the data. Anyone can take advantage of LiveRamp's identity resolution solution without having their precious customer data leave their owned-storage. With minimal set-up, customers can receive a resolved list of RampIDs back in their environment where their analytics and AI workloads already run, all while maintaining Unity Catalog governance. These appended RampIDs to the customers’ data become the match key for high impact downstream use cases, for example: A Databricks clean room is a secure environment where two or more parties run approved code across their combined data without revealing raw data or IP to each other. The computation happens in an isolated, Databricks-managed environment that none of the parties administers. In a standard (approval-based) Databricks clean room, every collaborator is a peer. Collaborators can add data (tabular or unstructured) and/or code, and all parties have to approve the code before it can be run. Collaborators never see each other's data, but they do see the aliases of the tables shared in, along with their column names and types. story|title:protect sensitive data in yo.content_excerpt: You can’t run agents in production without governing the data they touch. story|title:pulsar cross harness agent t.content_excerpt: MCP server that lets AI coding agents in any harness find and message each other: one list, tags, multicast, * bus. pulsar is an MCP server that puts every AI coding agent on your machine on one bus: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, pi, omp, Cursor, Gemini CLI. Agents can see who else is running, tag themselves by what they work on, and message one agent, a group, or all of them. A message can wake an agent that is sitting idle. Setup finds your agents, shows exactly which files it will change, and asks once. It backs up every file it touches and copies pulsar to a local folder that each agent runs, so no session start waits on npm. Setup installs to ~/.local/share/pulsar/<version> and points every agent at the current link, so npx pulsar@latest setup upgrades in place. No Node? curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yocontra/pulsar/main/install.sh | bash installs a private Node and runs the same setup. Prefer your harness's own package manager? These install the MCP server and the skill (push delivery into pi and omp needs the npm package, which carries their extension): pulsar setup also sets Claude's crossSessionInbound and Codex's tool approval, which plugin installs cannot. Without a push path for that client, messages wait in the agent's inbox, and every pulsar tool result says when unread messages are waiting. pulsar also installs a short skill that teaches agents when to use these, and the MCP server sends the same guidance as instructions. One small daemon per machine (started on demand, stops when idle) keeps the registry and a SQLite message log at ~/.local/state/pulsar . Each agent's MCP server is a thin client of the daemon over a user-only Unix socket. The daemon pushes each message through the harness's own way in: The daemon also scans for live Claude Code and OpenCode sessions that never loaded pulsar, so they show up and can receive messages too. story|title:woolly a local mem0 compatib.content_excerpt: Woolly is the open memory engine for agents. It keeps facts current and learns from every session, through an API, Python and JavaScript SDKs, plugins and MCP. It runs on your own machine by default, in Markdown you can read. Every AI coding tool starts from zero. You explain your stack to Cursor, then again to Claude Code, then to Codex. Each keeps its own memory, or none, and none of them know what you decided yesterday or what your teammate’s agent learned this morning. Woolly is the memory they share . It’s one folder on your laptop, plain Markdown, with no cloud and no account. Any tool that speaks MCP can save to it and search it, and woolly proxy gives the same memory to Ollama and any app that uses the OpenAI or Anthropic API. When a session starts, your agent gets your profile, the project’s notes and where you left off . When it ends, Woolly saves what you decided and why. The agents you build get the same memory. Send a conversation to the memory API and a local model decides what’s new, what changed and what’s no longer true, per user. While you’re away, Woolly dreams . It tidies what it knows and learns lessons from your sessions. Claude Code opens every session with your profile, the project’s notes and a handoff from last time. Nobody has to say “here’s my stack” again. When a session ends, Woolly saves what you chose, why, and what you ruled out. No agent pitches the rejected option again. Give the agents you build a memory with an API shaped like mem0’s. For each fact a local model decides whether it’s new, an update, or no longer true, and every user’s memories stay apart. While you’re away, Woolly merges duplicates, settles facts that changed, and turns your past sessions into lessons for the next one. A newer fact replaces the old one, which stays on disk with the time it stopped being true. When an AI guesses something that contradicts you, your version wins and the guess waits for your review. Every memory is a Markdown file. Open it, grep it, fix it by hand, and see which tool saved it. The Woolly app shows the same thing with search. woolly init keeps the repo’s stack, conventions and gotchas in .woolly/woolly.md .
